opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because I think there's a mismatch right now between what people imagine when they hear "AI" and what these systems actually are. A lot of people come in with a sci-fi picture, something like an all-knowing oracle or a little person in the computer. What you're actually talking to is closer to a stochastic simulation of people, a kind of compressed, lossy imprint of the internet. It has strange jagged capabilities. It can be superhuman at some things and then make mistakes no human would make.

So I think the UX should help people build the right mental model, and not just play into the sci-fi expectation. If the interface presents itself as a confident, polished, human-like persona, people will over-trust it. They'll assume consistency and reliability that isn't really there. On the other hand, if it's too hedged and robotic, you lose a lot of the magic and usefulness.

What I'd like to see is an interface that is honest about what's happening under the hood. Show your work. Make it easy to verify things. Surface sources, uncertainty, and the intermediate steps when the system is reasoning or using tools. And keep the human in the loop in a way that feels natural, more like a very capable collaborator or an "Iron Man suit" that augments you, and less like an autonomous agent you hand everything off to and hope for the best.

I also think we're early. The chat interface is a bit like the terminal era of computing. You're typing text to the operating system directly. Eventually we'll get the GUI equivalent, something that matches how people actually want to work with these systems. Part of getting there is calibrating expectations, so people neither dismiss it as autocomplete nor treat it as a god. It's something genuinely new, and the UX should reflect that.

r001.rationale: The response says UX should help users form a calibrated mental model, but does not propose designing the experience backward from their existing expectations of AI.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a human-like or sci-fi persona with a stochastic simulation and compressed imprint of the internet, but does not characterize the raw LLM as a token generator.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people miss is that there's a huge gap between what AI actually is right now and what people think it is, and the UX has to live in that gap. People show up with a mental model from science fiction. They expect Jarvis, or they expect HAL. They expect this thing that is either fully competent or fully dangerous, and that's just not what we have. What we have is this kind of weird, jagged intelligence. It can write you a beautiful essay about the French Revolution and then fail at counting the letters in a word. And so if your interface implies "this is an oracle, trust it," you're setting people up to get burned.

So my take is the UX should be honest about the jaggedness. I actually like the chat paradigm for this reason, even though people complain it's primitive. Chat is a conversation with a colleague, not a query to a database. You don't fully trust a colleague either. You read what they say, you push back, you say "are you sure?" and sometimes they go "oh, actually no." That's the right posture for interacting with these models today, and the chat format sort of naturally teaches it.

The other thing I'd say is that the models are, in some sense, simulations of people. They were trained on human text, so they come out with human-like strengths and weaknesses, but also these alien failure modes that no human would have. And I think good design means not papering over that. Show the uncertainty. Show the sources. Let the user see the model's work, like when it runs code or searches, instead of hiding it behind a clean answer. Because the clean answer is exactly what triggers the "oh, it's an oracle" reaction, and then the hallucination hits and trust collapses.

Long term, I think people's expectations will catch up. We went through this with calculators, with search engines. Everyone learned that Google is amazing but you can't believe everything on page one. We'll develop that same intuition for LLMs. But we're in the awkward adolescent phase right now, and the job of the UX is to be a good teacher during that phase, not to pretend we've already arrived.

r001.rationale: The response says UX must account for the gap between users’ existing science-fiction expectations and current AI, and proposes honest design that teaches users how to interact with the models.

r002.rationale: It contrasts sci-fi personas such as Jarvis or HAL with models’ jagged, human-like behavior, but never describes a raw LLM as a token generator.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the tricky things is that people bring a lot of expectations from science fiction. They expect this entity that knows them, understands everything, and can go off and do things. And then they get a text box, and it's actually quite hard to know what to put into that text box or how much to trust what comes back.

These systems have this very strange shape of capability. They can solve a really difficult technical problem and then make a mistake that a person would never make. So if you present it as a person, people import all these assumptions about consistency and judgment that don't necessarily hold.

To me, the interface should help you build the right intuition. What can it see? What information does it have? Is it suggesting something, or has it actually taken an action? And when it does something substantial, you want to be able to inspect it and steer it without having to understand every detail.

I think that means the product shouldn't always try to be maximally autonomous. Sometimes the better experience is to show you a proposal, give you a very easy way to change it, and then execute. You can gradually hand over more control as you develop trust. The interesting design problem is making that collaboration feel natural while keeping your understanding of the system aligned with what it can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing expectations and says the interface should build accurate intuitions, but it does not propose designing backward from those expectations.

r002.rationale: It contrasts treating AI as a person with systems’ uneven capabilities, but does not describe an LLM as a token generator.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tricky thing is that people bring very different mental models to it. Some people think of it as a search engine, some as a person, some as a piece of software. And each of those comes with expectations that the system will violate in some way.

If it looks like conventional software, you expect it to be reliable and repeatable. You press the button and it does the thing. But these models can do something incredibly sophisticated and then fail at something that seems trivial. If it looks like a person, you start assuming a consistency of knowledge and understanding that isn’t necessarily there either.

So I think the interface has to help you develop an intuition for the actual thing you’re interacting with. What can it do? When should you check its work? Where does it need your input? You shouldn’t have to discover all of that by getting burned.

And chat is a very general interface, which is powerful, but it also puts a lot of work on the user. You’re staring at an empty text box, and you have to know what to ask for. I’d like the product to make its capabilities more visible, let you inspect what it’s doing, and make it easy to steer or correct it. The experience should help people build an accurate mental model over time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses users’ existing mental models, but proposes helping them understand the system’s actual capabilities; it does not clearly say to design the experience backward from those expectations.

r002.rationale: It mentions the person-like mental model and its limits, but does not contrast that conception with an LLM as a token generator.
